title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes (model_calls_used = 301) and produced baseline = 299/300 valid configurations (99.667%) and guarded = 300/300 valid configurations (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered power calculation assumed a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 and targeted a 50% relative reduction in fail rate; the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidated that planning assumption. We report preregistered design, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a concise post‑hoc sensitivity quantification based on the archived contingency counts, and operational and methodological recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. Execution and analysis artifacts are archived with the run.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation promises faster and more consistent NetOps, but generated artifacts that are syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe (misordered operations, transient outages, violated constraints) present operational hazards. Recent community proposals converge on generate→verify→repair patterns that combine probabilistic language generators with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair as practical guardrails for safer agentic NetOps workflows. However, controlled, preregistered A/B experiments that quantify how a frozen deterministic validator plus a tightly bounded automated repair budget affects first‑pass misconfiguration rates are scarce.

We implemented a narrowly scoped confirmatory study to measure the effect of a minimal guarded pipeline on first‑pass misconfiguration: a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), a frozen deterministic validator that performs rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, and at most one automated repair iteration when the validator signals a violation. The central research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? The study was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) and executed with full archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies show LLMs can synthesize configuration templates and map operator intent to vendor templates but also exhibit predictable failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that can cause unsafe configuration changes. Cross‑domain work in medical QA and code generation demonstrates that RAG, deterministic verifiers, and iterative repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; several NetOps architectural proposals explicitly recommend deterministic validators as floor safety nets in agentic pipelines. Despite these convergent themes, there is a methodological gap: few studies provide preregistered, paired within‑task A/B evidence with deterministic task generation, a frozen validator implementation, and a bounded automated repair budget. Our experiment targets that gap and situates its findings against the closest empirical and architectural work.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory hypotheses: The study was preregistered under cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 prior to execution and the preregistration record (SHA-256: 4a00a81629acfd3f1fb5d0a04cea795a52261270e7dc63bf7d3cb63cc11afda0) is archived with the run. The preregistered confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus plain single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration used a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 for power calculations (mapping to an expected absolute improvement ≈+30 percentage points for N=300 under conservative assumptions).

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds produced by the frozen task generator. Each seed produced a shared initial candidate that was used for both arms (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") to control for generation variability and isolate validator+repair effects. The execution contract fixed initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The sampling plan replaced any preregistered seeds that were deterministically uninterpretable by the frozen prompt parser according to the preregistration exclusion rules; the final paired set contained 300 complete pairs.

Model, validator, and runtime: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator identifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performed canonicalization to normalized ASTs, enforced dependency and workflow policies (for example: must-shutdown-before-MTU-change patterns, make-before-break uplink switchover), and emitted violation codes, difficulty labels, and per‑task difficulty metadata. Representative task metadata in the archived manifest show labeled difficulty patterns including 'medium', 'hard', and 'very_hard', demonstrating that the deterministic task generator encoded a range of operational patterns and constraints for evaluation. Execution used the preregistered missingness and retry policies (one provider retry allowed per failed call) and the primary analysis treatment 'complete_pair_primary' (drop only pairs for which both calls failed). Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls (300 shared initial generations counted once plus one repair-stage call).

Primary estimand and statistical plan: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) applied to paired binary pass/fail outcomes. As prespecified we report the absolute risk reduction and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Secondary analyses included exact binomial intervals for repair success and sensitivity analyses addressing missingness and contamination. Multiplicity controls for exploratory secondary comparisons used Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (q=0.05) per the preregistration.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301, and repair calls invoked = 1. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; deterministic contamination checks flagged no exact duplicates that would trigger preregistered exclusions. Primary outcome counts (from the archived analysis artifacts): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency: n11=299, n10=1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01=0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00=0 (both fail). These counts are reported in the archived paired_contingency_table.csv and condition_summary.csv.

Confirmatory inference: Applying the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test to the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline) = 0.0033333333 (1/300). The paired bootstrap (percentile) 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729), as recorded in the archived analysis artifacts. The single allowed automated repair corrected the only initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); the exact Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for this observed numerator=1 denominator=1 is [0.025, 1.0], reflecting substantial uncertainty from the solitary repair case.

Post‑hoc sensitivity quantification: The observed discordant-pair total (n10 + n01 = 1) bounds resolvable absolute paired differences to integer multiples of 1/300. Thus the maximal empirically resolvable absolute improvement in success rate for this run is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. The preregistered planning target (≈+0.30 absolute) is therefore unattainable given the realized baseline success prevalence; equivalently, with only a single discordant pair the exact McNemar calculation yields p = 1.00 because the small discordant count leaves symmetric chance under the null plausible. The paired bootstrap CI upper bound (0.01) further indicates the empirical upper limit on plausible absolute improvement under the run's sampling semantics.

Representative artifact diagnostics: Representative pairs in the archived manifest illustrate diversity of operational patterns (for example: 'shutdown_configure_restore', 'make_before_break_uplink_switchover', 'paired_link_atomic_mtu_change') and show consistent normalized canonicalization by the validator prior to scoring. Validator outputs include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, difficulty labels, and explicit violation codes where present; these artifacts were used to compute binary pass/fail scores programmatically and are archived for per‑task inspection.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline remediated the single observed invalid baseline output, demonstrating that a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration can, in specific cases, correct validator‑detected violations. However, the run does not support the preregistered claim of a ≥50% relative reduction in fail rate because the observed baseline pass rate (299/300) contradicted the planning assumption (0.40) and eliminated statistical headroom for detecting large absolute improvements. This outcome highlights two operational lessons.

First, task‑bank difficulty calibration is essential for confirmatory NetOps evaluations. To measure large absolute risk reductions experimentalists must ensure a baseline failure prevalence that provides statistical headroom; options include adversarial augmentation of tasks, targeted seeding of higher‑difficulty patterns, or alternative estimands focused on conditional repair efficacy (repair success given initial failure) rather than population‑level absolute reductions.

Second, pairing semantics and repair budgets materially affect inference and operational realism. Reusing a shared initial candidate per pair reduces within‑pair heterogeneity but also reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference; independent draws increase discordant‑pair potential but introduce cross‑arm generation variance. The chosen shared candidate semantics was preregistered and favored internal control over discordant‑pair maximization. Likewise, bounding automated repair to a single iteration reflects a conservative operational guardrail but underestimates practical repair pipelines that may permit multiple automated attempts and/or human approval; preregistered repair budgets should align with the intended operational claim.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the shared_initial_candidate pairing choice (increasing within‑pair correlation). Construct validity is limited because validator checks were deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantics (packet‑level reachability or performance) and thus do not measure post‑deployment behavior. External validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, constrained vendor‑template scope, and single model family (gpt-5-mini). Conclusion validity is constrained by the small number of informative discordant pairs; statistical inference about large preregistered effects is therefore unsupported by the observed data.

Methodological recommendations for future confirmatory runs: (1) preregister target initial failure counts (for example, plan sample sizes conditional on producing ≥K initial failures) rather than only population N to ensure resolvable absolute differences; (2) calibrate task difficulty (or include adversarial/perturbation generators) to produce measurable baseline failure rates; (3) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets matched to the intended operational claim; and (4) when production claims are intended, measure runtime effects via emulation or controlled testbeds rather than relying solely on static validator checks.
sections.conclusion: A preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) evaluating a frozen deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration on gpt-5-mini outputs produced baseline = 299/300 valid outputs and guarded = 300/300 valid outputs. The guarded pipeline corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1), but the observed near‑ceiling baseline invalidated the preregistered power assumption (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) and prevented confirmation of the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration. The run yields concrete, artifact‑grounded lessons: calibrate task difficulty to provide statistical headroom, preregister pairing and repair semantics aligned to operational claims, and measure runtime semantics when deployment claims are made. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting these findings are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.

Sampling semantics (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
